headline: How HGH
punch: There are two routes. Your blood test sees one.

headline: Your pituitary is nowhere
body: So lets start with the thing most people get wrong about growth hormone. GH is made in your pituitary gland, which sits underneath your brain. Your growth plates are down in your legs. There is no version of this where GH reaches down and physically lengthens a bone. | What it does instead is give orders to other things, and there are two completely separate routes those orders travel down. One of them is on your bloodwork. The other one is not, and that is the entire point of this post.
punch: ==GH gives the order. It does not do the job.==

headline: Route one
body: GH travels in your blood to your liver and tells it to produce *IGF-1*, which stands for insulin-like growth factor 1. The liver pumps that IGF-1 back out into circulation, it travels to the growth plate, and it tells the cartilage cells there to divide. | This is the route everybody knows about, and it is the route your blood test measures when it gives you an IGF-1 number. So far the model everyone uses is correct. The problem is that it is only half of what is happening.
punch: Your IGF-1 number is reporting on route one.

headline: Route two
body: GH also travels directly to the growth plate itself and acts on the cells there, without going anywhere near your liver first. Lundberg 2015 states it plainly: GH has effects on longitudinal bone growth **both directly at the growth plate and locally mediated through IGF-1**. | And the plate makes its own IGF-1 in response, right there in the tissue, used in the same place it is made. That local pool never enters general circulation in a way a blood test can see.
punch: _Two routes. One of them is invisible on a blood test._

headline: They do different jobs
body: Hunziker 1994 measured exactly how each one acts. They took rats with no pituitary, gave them either IGF-1 or GH, and measured how long one cell cycle takes in the *stem cells*, meaning the reserve layer sitting at the very top of the growth plate. | Untreated those cells took **50 days** per division. With IGF-1 it dropped to **15 days**. With GH it dropped to **8 days**, where a normal rat sits at 6. | What this means is that both hormones speed up the reserve layer, and GH speeds it up considerably more.
punch: GH hits the reserve layer hardest.

headline: The reserve layer
body: Here is why that matters more than it sounds. The reserve cells at the top of the plate divide and feed every layer beneath them. Every dividing cell and every swelling cell further down started as one of those. | So if you speed up the reserve layer, the entire plate produces more, all the way down. That is the actual mechanism behind height on this axis. Not GH stretching a bone, but GH making the cell factory at the top of the plate run faster than it otherwise would.
punch: ==The top of the plate is the factory. GH speeds up the factory.==

headline: Can you overdo it?
body: This is where it stops being a story about more is better. In that same rat study, when **the maximal chosen dose of GH was exceeded, growth plate height did not remain stable but decreased**. | So in an animal model with no cost, no side effects and no budget, pushing past a certain point made the plate physically worse rather than better. The response curve bends and then it turns over. That is the single most useful fact in this whole post.
punch: More is not linearly better. It bends.

headline: How do we use this?
body: Three things hold up. GH works through two routes, one through your liver and one straight into the plate. It works mainly by speeding up the reserve cells at the top, which feed everything below. And the dose response bends rather than climbing forever. | Which means your IGF-1 result is reporting on exactly one of the two routes, and the one it cannot see is the one acting directly on the tissue you care about.
punch: Your blood test sees half the story.
